Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a fungal disease (Venturia inaequalis) causing olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit, often leading to early leaf drop.
Apple___Apple_scab.treatment: Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves at season's end to reduce next year's spore source; prune for better airflow.
Apple___Apple_scab.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes dense, humid foliage favorable to scab.
Apple___Apple_scab.pesticide_guidance: Preventive fungicide programs (e.g. captan or sulfur-based, where locally approved) are commonly used starting at bud break; follow local label directions.
Apple___Apple_scab.prevention: Choose scab-resistant apple varieties where possible; avoid overhead irrigation.
Apple___Apple_scab.crop_management: Prune to open the canopy for sunlight and airflow, which speeds leaf drying after rain.
Apple___Apple_scab.monitoring_advice: Inspect new leaves and fruit weekly during wet spring weather, when scab spreads fastest.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot (Botryosphaeria obtusa) causes purple-bordered leaf spots and can rot fruit and cankers on branches.
Apple___Black_rot.treatment: Prune out dead wood and cankers; remove mummified fruit left on the tree or ground, which harbor the fungus.
Apple___Black_rot.fertilizer: Maintain balanced tree nutrition; avoid stressing the tree, which increases susceptibility.
Apple___Black_rot.pesticide_guidance: Fungicide programs used for apple scab often also help manage black rot; consult local guidance for timing.
Apple___Black_rot.prevention: Remove nearby dead or infected wood promptly; avoid wounding bark during maintenance.
Apple___Black_rot.crop_management: Ensure good pruning practices for airflow and sunlight penetration.
Apple___Black_rot.monitoring_advice: Check branches and fruit regularly, especially after storm damage that creates entry wounds.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae) causes bright orange-yellow spots on leaves; it requires both apple and a nearby juniper/cedar host to complete its life cycle.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.treatment: Remove nearby juniper/cedar hosts within a few hundred meters if feasible, as they harbor the overwintering stage.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition; this disease is not fertilizer-related.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.pesticide_guidance: Preventive fungicide applications in spring (where locally approved) can reduce infection during the spore-release period.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties where cedar/juniper hosts are common nearby.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.crop_management: Monitor nearby juniper plants for the orange gelatinous galls that release spores in spring.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.monitoring_advice: Check leaves in spring, especially after rain, when spores are released from nearby junipers.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew appears as white, powdery fungal growth on leaves and shoots, thriving in warm, dry conditions with high humidity at night.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.treatment: Prune out heavily infected shoots; improve airflow through the canopy.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which encourages the succulent new growth mildew prefers.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.pesticide_guidance: Sulfur-based or other locally approved fungicides are commonly used against powdery mildew; follow label directions.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Space and prune trees for airflow; avoid overhead irrigation in the evening.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.crop_management: Remove water sprouts and dense inner growth during dormant pruning.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.monitoring_advice: Check new shoot tips weekly in warm weather, where mildew often starts.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust (Puccinia sorghi) produces small, reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces; it's usually less damaging than southern rust but can reduce yield in heavy infections.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.treatment: Most common corn hybrids tolerate common rust well; treatment is rarely needed unless infection is severe and early.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition to support plant vigor.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.pesticide_guidance: Fungicide is rarely justified for common rust alone; consult a local expert if pustule density is very high on young plants.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.prevention: Most modern hybrids have adequate resistance; select resistant varieties in high-pressure areas.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.crop_management: No special management typically needed beyond routine monitoring.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.monitoring_advice: Scout periodically; heavy pustule coverage on upper leaves before tasseling is the main concern.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight (Exserohilum turcicum) causes long, elliptical gray-green to tan lesions on leaves, which can merge and cause significant leaf loss in humid conditions.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.treatment: Remove or bury infected residue after harvest to limit carryover to the next season.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nitrogen; nutrient-stressed plants show more severe symptoms.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.pesticide_guidance: Foliar fungicides may be warranted in susceptible hybrids under high disease pressure; consult local extension timing guidance.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.prevention: Choose resistant hybrids; rotate away from continuous corn where feasible.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.crop_management: Reduce residue buildup and consider tillage practices that speed residue breakdown in high-risk fields.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.monitoring_advice: Scout weekly from mid-vegetative stage onward, especially in humid, overcast weather.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot (Guignardia bidwellii) causes reddish-brown leaf spots and can mummify grape berries; it thrives in warm, wet conditions.
Grape___Black_rot.treatment: Remove mummified berries and infected leaves/canes, which are the main source of spores for the next season.
Grape___Black_rot.fertilizer: Maintain balanced vine nutrition; avoid excess vigor that reduces airflow.
Grape___Black_rot.pesticide_guidance: Preventive fungicide programs from early shoot growth through fruit set (where locally approved) are commonly used.
Grape___Black_rot.prevention: Prune for an open canopy; remove wild/abandoned grapevines nearby that can harbor the fungus.
Grape___Black_rot.crop_management: Practice canopy management (shoot thinning, leaf pulling) to improve sunlight and airflow.
Grape___Black_rot.monitoring_advice: Inspect leaves and clusters weekly during wet spring weather.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca (a complex of wood-rotting fungi) causes tiger-stripe leaf discoloration and can lead to vine decline over years; it's associated with pruning wounds and older wood.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).treatment: There is no cure once wood is infected; remove and destroy severely affected vines/wood, and avoid pruning in wet weather.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).fertilizer: Maintain balanced vine nutrition to support overall vine health and resilience.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).pesticide_guidance: No reliable curative fungicide exists for esca; management focuses on prevention. Consult a viticulture expert for severe cases.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).prevention: Protect pruning wounds, prune in dry weather, and avoid large pruning cuts on older wood where possible.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).crop_management: Consider retraining/replacing chronically affected vines over time.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).monitoring_advice: Watch for the characteristic tiger-stripe leaf pattern in mid-to-late summer, which often signals internal wood decay.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Isariopsis leaf blight causes angular, dark brown spots on grape leaves, sometimes leading to premature defoliation in warm, humid climates.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.treatment: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves; improve canopy airflow through pruning.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition; avoid excess nitrogen that promotes dense canopy humidity.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.pesticide_guidance: Fungicide programs used for other grape leaf diseases often provide some control; consult local guidance.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.prevention: Prune for airflow; avoid working in wet canopies, which can spread spores.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.crop_management: Practice canopy management to reduce humidity within the vine.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.monitoring_advice: Check leaves regularly during warm, humid periods.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing / HLB) is a serious bacterial disease spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, causing blotchy mottled leaves, lopsided bitter fruit, and eventual tree decline. There is no cure.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).treatment: There is no cure for HLB. Infected trees should be reported to and removed under local agricultural authority guidance to slow regional spread.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).fertilizer: Enhanced nutritional programs are sometimes used to prolong productivity of infected trees, but they do not cure the disease — follow local extension guidance.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pesticide_guidance: Psyllid vector control (insecticide programs targeting the Asian citrus psyllid) is the primary management tool; consult a local citrus extension program, as this is a regulated disease in many regions.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).prevention: Use certified disease-free nursery stock; control psyllid populations; remove confirmed infected trees promptly per local regulations.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).crop_management: This is a serious regulated disease — contact your local agricultural extension or plant health authority immediately if HLB is suspected.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).monitoring_advice: Inspect new flush growth regularly for blotchy mottling and monitor for psyllid activity.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot (Xanthomonas arboricola) causes small, dark, angular spots on leaves that may fall out leaving a 'shot-hole' look, and can also spot fruit.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves and twigs; avoid working in wet orchards, which spreads bacteria.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes susceptible new growth.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.pesticide_guidance: Copper-based bactericides (where locally approved) applied preventively are commonly used; bacterial diseases do not respond to fungicides.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Choose resistant peach varieties where available; avoid overhead irrigation.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.crop_management: Prune for airflow and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.monitoring_advice: Inspect leaves after wind-driven rain, which spreads the bacteria.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot (Xanthomonas species) causes small, water-soaked, dark leaf spots that can merge, and scabby spots on fruit; it spreads rapidly in warm, wet, windy conditions.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Remove and destroy infected plant debris; avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet plants.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition; avoid excess nitrogen.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.pesticide_guidance: Copper-based bactericides (where locally approved) may reduce spread if applied early; bacterial diseases do not respond to fungicides.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed/transplants; rotate away from peppers/tomatoes for 1-2 seasons.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.crop_management: Space plants for airflow; avoid handling wet plants to reduce mechanical spread.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.monitoring_advice: Inspect leaves every few days during warm, wet, or windy weather.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight (Alternaria solani) causes dark, concentric-ringed 'target' spots on older leaves first, typically starting mid-season.
Potato___Early_blight.treatment: Remove and destroy affected lower leaves; ensure adequate plant nutrition to support regrowth.
Potato___Early_blight.fertilizer: Avoid nitrogen deficiency, which increases susceptibility; maintain balanced potassium levels.
Potato___Early_blight.pesticide_guidance: Chlorothalonil or copper-based fungicides (where locally approved) are commonly used; follow local label directions and pre-harvest intervals.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention: Rotate crops away from potato/tomato family for 2+ seasons; use certified disease-free seed potatoes.
Potato___Early_blight.crop_management: Ensure adequate plant spacing and hilling for airflow.
Potato___Early_blight.monitoring_advice: Check lower/older leaves every few days once symptoms are suspected; the disease moves upward over time.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) causes water-soaked lesions that spread rapidly in cool, wet conditions and can destroy a crop within days — this is the pathogen behind historic potato famines.
Potato___Late_blight.treatment: This disease spreads fast — remove and destroy infected plants promptly; do not compost infected material.
Potato___Late_blight.fertilizer: Focus on plant recovery post-outbreak with balanced fertilization; avoid stimulating excess soft new growth mid-outbreak.
Potato___Late_blight.pesticide_guidance: Late blight often requires prompt, expert-guided fungicide intervention (e.g. products containing mancozeb or chlorothalonil, where locally approved); consult a local expert given how fast this disease spreads.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes; avoid overhead irrigation; monitor weather for the cool, humid conditions that favor outbreaks.
Potato___Late_blight.crop_management: Increase plant spacing and remove volunteer potato/tomato plants that can harbor the pathogen between seasons.
Potato___Late_blight.monitoring_advice: Check daily during cool, wet weather — this disease can move from a few spots to total crop loss within a week.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew appears as white powdery patches on squash leaves and stems, common in warm, humid climates, and can reduce yield if severe.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.treatment: Remove heavily infected leaves; improve airflow by thinning dense foliage.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes dense, susceptible foliage.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.pesticide_guidance: Sulfur-based or potassium bicarbonate fungicides (where locally approved) are commonly used against powdery mildew.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Choose resistant varieties where available; space plants for airflow.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.crop_management: Water at the base of plants rather than overhead; avoid overcrowding.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.monitoring_advice: Check the undersides of leaves weekly, especially in warm, humid weather.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch (Diplocarpon earlianum) causes small purple spots that merge into larger scorched-looking blotches on strawberry leaves.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves after harvest (a common renovation practice); avoid overhead irrigation.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition; avoid excess nitrogen that promotes dense, humid foliage.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.pesticide_guidance: Fungicide programs (where locally approved) may help in high-pressure plantings; consult local guidance on timing.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.prevention: Use disease-free transplants; renovate beds (mow and remove old leaves) after harvest each year.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.crop_management: Space plants for airflow and avoid working in wet foliage.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.monitoring_advice: Inspect leaves regularly through the growing season, especially after rain.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot (Xanthomonas species) causes small, dark, water-soaked leaf spots and scabby fruit lesions; it spreads rapidly in warm, wet, windy conditions.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Remove and destroy infected plant debris; avoid overhead irrigation and handling wet plants.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition; avoid excess nitrogen.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.pesticide_guidance: Copper-based bactericides (where locally approved) may reduce spread if applied early; this is a bacterial disease and does not respond to fungicides.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed/transplants; rotate away from tomatoes/peppers for 1-2 seasons.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.crop_management: Space plants for airflow; stake to keep foliage off the ground.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.monitoring_advice: Inspect leaves every few days during warm, wet, or windy weather.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a fungal disease (Alternaria solani) causing dark concentric-ringed spots on older leaves first.
Tomato___Early_blight.treatment: Remove and destroy affected lower leaves; improve airflow via pruning and spacing.
Tomato___Early_blight.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes dense foliage and humidity around leaves; ensure adequate potassium.
Tomato___Early_blight.pesticide_guidance: Copper-based or chlorothalonil-based fungicides are commonly used against early blight; follow local label directions and pre-harvest intervals.
Tomato___Early_blight.prevention: Rotate crops away from tomato/potato family for 2+ seasons; use disease-free transplants; mulch to reduce soil splash onto leaves.
Tomato___Early_blight.crop_management: Stake or cage plants to keep foliage off the ground; water at the base, not overhead.
Tomato___Early_blight.monitoring_advice: Check lower leaves every 3-4 days once symptoms are suspected; blight spreads upward over time.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) causes water-soaked lesions that spread rapidly in cool, wet conditions and can destroy a crop within days.
Tomato___Late_blight.treatment: This disease spreads fast — remove and destroy infected plants promptly; do not compost infected material.
Tomato___Late_blight.fertilizer: Focus on plant recovery once the outbreak is controlled; avoid stimulating excess soft new growth mid-outbreak.
Tomato___Late_blight.pesticide_guidance: Late blight often requires prompt, expert-guided fungicide intervention (e.g. products containing mancozeb or chlorothalonil, where locally approved); consult a local expert given how fast this disease spreads.
Tomato___Late_blight.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed/transplants; avoid overhead irrigation; monitor weather for the cool, humid conditions that favor outbreaks.
Tomato___Late_blight.crop_management: Increase plant spacing and remove volunteer potato/tomato plants that can harbor the pathogen between seasons.
Tomato___Late_blight.monitoring_advice: Check daily during cool, wet weather — this disease can move from a few spots to total crop loss within a week.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mold (Passalora fulva) causes pale green-to-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces with an olive-green to grayish-purple fuzzy mold underneath; it's especially common in humid greenhouse conditions.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves; increase ventilation to lower humidity around plants.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition; this disease is driven mainly by humidity, not fertility.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.pesticide_guidance: Fungicides (where locally approved) can help in persistent cases; improving ventilation is usually the priority for greenhouse growers.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.prevention: Choose resistant varieties where available; avoid overhead watering and overcrowding.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.crop_management: Improve airflow (ventilation, plant spacing, pruning lower leaves) to reduce humidity around foliage.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.monitoring_advice: Check leaf undersides weekly, especially in humid or poorly ventilated growing spaces.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot (Septoria lycopersici) causes small, circular spots with dark borders and light centers, usually starting on lower leaves and spreading upward.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves promptly; avoid overhead watering.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition to support plant vigor and recovery.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.pesticide_guidance: Chlorothalonil or copper-based fungicides (where locally approved) are commonly used; follow local label directions.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: Rotate crops away from tomato family for 1-2 seasons; mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.crop_management: Stake plants and remove lower leaves that touch the soil.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.monitoring_advice: Check lower leaves every few days, especially after rain — this disease spreads upward quickly.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny pests (not a disease) causing stippled, yellowing leaves and fine webbing, especially in hot, dry conditions.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.treatment: Rinse plants with a strong water spray to dislodge mites; remove heavily infested leaves.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which can increase mite reproduction on lush growth.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.pesticide_guidance: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil (where locally approved) can help; avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that also kill mite predators.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.prevention: Keep plants adequately watered — drought-stressed plants are more attractive to spider mites.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.crop_management: Encourage natural predators (e.g. predatory mites, ladybugs) by minimizing broad-spectrum pesticide use.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.monitoring_advice: Check the undersides of leaves for fine webbing and stippling, especially during hot, dry spells.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot (Corynespora cassiicola) causes brown lesions with concentric rings, resembling early blight, and can affect leaves, stems, and fruit in warm, humid conditions.
Tomato___Target_Spot.treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves; improve airflow around plants.
Tomato___Target_Spot.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition to support plant vigor.
Tomato___Target_Spot.pesticide_guidance: Fungicides used for other tomato leaf spot diseases (where locally approved) often provide some control; consult local guidance.
Tomato___Target_Spot.prevention: Rotate crops; avoid overhead irrigation; use disease-free transplants.
Tomato___Target_Spot.crop_management: Stake plants and prune for airflow, avoiding dense, humid canopies.
Tomato___Target_Spot.monitoring_advice: Check leaves and fruit regularly during warm, humid weather.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is spread by whiteflies and causes upward-curling, yellowing leaves and stunted growth; there is no cure once a plant is infected.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.treatment: There is no cure — remove and destroy infected plants to reduce the source of infection for whiteflies to spread further.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.fertilizer: Not fertilizer-related; focus fertility efforts on healthy remaining plants.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pesticide_guidance: Manage the whitefly vector (insecticidal soap, reflective mulches, or approved insecticides) rather than the virus itself, which has no direct treatment.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.prevention: Use virus-resistant tomato varieties where available; control whitefly populations; use insect netting on young transplants.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.crop_management: Remove and destroy infected plants promptly rather than allowing them to remain as a whitefly source.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.monitoring_advice: Monitor for whitefly activity and early leaf curling/yellowing symptoms, especially in warm weather.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) causes mottled light/dark green mosaic patterns on leaves, sometimes with leaf curling and stunted growth; it spreads easily through contact, tools, and hands.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment: There is no cure — remove and destroy infected plants. Wash hands and disinfect tools after handling infected plants before touching healthy ones.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.fertilizer: Not fertilizer-related; maintain balanced nutrition on remaining healthy plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.pesticide_guidance: Not applicable — this is a virus, not a pest or fungal issue; sanitation is the primary control.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention: Use certified virus-free seed; avoid tobacco product use near plants (a known transmission route); disinfect tools between plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.crop_management: Avoid working with wet plants and disinfect hands/tools between handling different plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.monitoring_advice: Watch for mottled mosaic leaf patterns and isolate/remove suspect plants promptly.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot (Cercospora zeae-maydis) causes rectangular gray-to-tan lesions running parallel to leaf veins, most severe in warm, humid conditions with heavy crop residue.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.treatment: Remove or bury heavily infected crop residue after harvest to reduce the disease's overwintering source.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nitrogen; stressed, nutrient-deficient plants are more susceptible.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.pesticide_guidance: Foliar fungicides (e.g. strobilurin or triazole-based, where locally approved) may be warranted in high-risk fields; consult local extension guidance on timing.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.prevention: Rotate away from continuous corn where feasible; choose resistant hybrids.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.crop_management: Reduce plant density in high-risk fields to improve airflow and leaf drying.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.monitoring_advice: Scout fields weekly starting mid-season, focusing on lower leaves first.
